articles.title: Do Nice Guys (and Gals) Really Finish Last? Here’s What the Science Actually Says
articles.content:
Oh, you are so nice! I used to consider being “nice” as the ultimate compliment. I wanted to be the kind of person that people described as nice, even when I wasn’t in the room.
Which brings me to one of my favorite employment stories: My boss needed help getting a bunch of shifts covered during a very busy season, and I volunteered. Because I’m a team player! Because I genuinely like helping people! And, if I’m being completely honest, because I thought if I was just nice enough, I could get on her good side and get promoted.
For months, I burned myself out, working early and late shifts on top of my own workload. Then one day, I finally got an email from my boss. I assumed it was going to be something like: “Thank you so much for all the extra work you’ve been putting in. I couldn’t do this without you!” Nope. Instead, she scolded me for not cleaning enough after one shift and ended with the line: “Don’t forget—working here is a privilege.” My brain exploded.
Y’all, it was a minimum-wage job.
I was not working as a peacekeeper for the U.N. I was not curing childhood cancer. I was not following the president around with a briefcase of nuclear codes handcuffed to my wrist. And the truth was that I was doing her a favor for basically the price of a cup of coffee (and my dignity)!
Not only did being nice not get me a promotion—it didn’t even get me recognized as a good human being. But the part that stung the worst? The person who did get the promotion was the definition of Not Nice. It was one of the moments where you start to understand why people say nice guys finish last. (Or in my case, nice gals work 50 extra shifts, clean the bathroom, organize the equipment, get an ulcer and then apologize for leaving some boxes out … because that’s what I did.)
But still, being nice is a good thing, right? We see how awesome it can be time and again in Reader’s Digest‘s annual Nicest Places in America search. And let’s be honest: No one wants to hang out with (or date) a jerk. But do nice guys really finish last? It turns out that science does have an answer, but it’s complicated. And it starts with defining what “nice” really is.
Read on to find out what actually qualifies as being nice and what it can lead to—if you do it the right way.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more life tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
For starters, “nice” doesn’t mean being a doormat, says Adam Mendler, PhD, who teaches graduate-level leadership courses at UCLA and hosts the Thirty Minute Mentors podcast, where he regularly advises people on how to be both nice and successful. “Kindness can signal to people that you’re soft or a pushover,” he says. “Some people will try to see how far they can push you or what they can get away with.”
Eliska Kostelny, PsyD, a licensed clinical professional counselor and clinical supervisor at Pure Health Center, adds another concern to the mix: “Being nice” can be seen as not being proactive or passionate.
OK, so what does it really mean to be nice? The word is actually so nebulous and used in so many different contexts—good and bad—that researchers often avoid it, says Christian Bumpous, a licensed psychotherapist and the founder of Therapie in Nashville.
So instead of researching niceness, scientists instead tend to look at “agreeableness,” a Big Five trait that includes trust, straightforwardness, altruism, compliance, modesty and tender-mindedness—or “kindness,” which the Kindlab defines as “an action intended to benefit someone else at some cost to yourself.”
It depends entirely on the setting. When people talk about nice guys finishing last, it’s usually in the context of pay/promotions at work, love and overall happiness. And the answer changes depending on which one of those three things you’re measuring. For instance, the agreeable type of “nice” is sometimes linked with poorer work outcomes, while true kindness is linked to more successful relationships, better reputations and increased well-being. Here’s how it breaks down.
In a classic study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researchers found that overall agreeable people do earn less over the course of their careers—and the effect was stronger for men. “The researchers assumed it was likely because they negotiate and advocate for themselves less than less-nice peers,” Bumpous says. “A person can end up avoiding conflict and saying yes too often. They tend to undernegotiate and get overlooked for raises and promotions at work. Over time, that can build resentment, which in turn leads to increased stress and feelings of burnout.”
However, while the research focuses on agreeableness, Mendler says that kindness produces different results because people who are kind are likable. “People would rather work with, hire, promote and support someone they like and trust,” he says. “Over the years, I have been given opportunities I wasn’t the best candidate for because the decision-maker liked me, and a big part of being likable is being kind.”
Research backs that up: A study published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin found that strangers placed in random groups were most likely to choose the most altruistic group members to be both leaders and partners. So if your work involves leadership or working with others, being kind is a must.
“Kindness leads to stronger trust in relationships, more loyalty, and increased social support,” Bumpous says. “All three things can be protective factors that ultimately buffer stress. It also leads to better teamwork and a better reputation at work over time.”
Despite what the internet may tell you, kind men are not finishing last in love. In fact, it’s quite the opposite. A foundational study published in 2003 found that women prefer men who come across as kind and sensitive over those who are jerks—even when the jerk was rated as more attractive. A follow-up study of 191 male college students found that men who scored lower in agreeableness were more likely to have casual, less-committed sexual relationships. So if you’re looking for real romance, being nice is the way to go.
Bumpous references the decades of research on relationships done by the Gottman Institute: “They found kindness is one of the strongest predictors when it comes to stable partnerships. In the long run, being nice works out.”
Of course, romance is only one type of relationship, and a fulfilling life has many types of close connections. “We also often see the ‘nice guy’ archetype as the unrequited, friend-zoned person who is overlooked by their romantic interest, who instead pursues the ‘bad boy,’” Kostelny says. “In reality, truly nice people rarely finish last, because they are more likely to create community and friendships that result in life satisfaction.”
Nice people are happier. Why? The primary driver of happiness is meaningful relationships, according to the Harvard Longevity Study, the longest-running study on happiness in the world. “Typically, kind people tend to be happier and can form more durable friendships, and they also have stronger romantic relationships,” Bumpous says. “Overall, kindness is linked to higher well-being for the person who’s being kind.”
It is also true that being kind—as in selflessly helping someone else—has been linked over and over in the research to more feelings of happiness. In a 2018 meta-analysis that reviewed 27 experiments involving more than 4,000 people, researchers found that people who performed acts of kindness reported significantly higher well-being than those who didn’t.
Usually not, but the ones who do tend to be either pushovers or are being performatively nice. The latter is when people are being kind … but also looking to get something out of it vs. doing it selflessly. Looking back at my experience, I can see now that I was being both a pushover and performatively nice. So perhaps it’s not surprising that I didn’t get the result I was looking for. But when you’re looking at success, it’s important to play the long game.
“In the short term, aggressive or selfish behavior can pay off, making it look like the nice guy finished last, but in the long run, your reputation catches up with you,” Mendler says. “People remember who treated them well, who treated them poorly and who was only nice when they wanted something.”
Yes, but it’s mostly in how they’re judged by other people, not in how nice they actually are. “There is a definite difference in expectations,” Mendler says. “Aggressive and assertive behavior is often rewarded in men and penalized in women.” He explains that a man who pushes hard may be viewed as strong, while a woman who behaves the same way may be viewed as difficult.
Women are also generally expected to be more accommodating and conflict-averse. As a result, women in the workplace can be looked down on both for being too soft and for not being soft enough. “It is a double standard that many well-meaning people are not aware of,” he says.
But men can be negatively affected by these stereotypes as well. “On the flip side, nice men can be seen as less dominant or soft,’ so both genders can get punished,” Bumpous says. “It just shows up in different ways.”
It’s about being kind while also having boundaries—and those boundaries need to be nonnegotiable. Now, it’s important to say that setting limits does not mean you’re being mean. “A kind person helps because they want to,” Mendler explains. “A pushover helps because they don’t feel comfortable saying no.”
Bumpous adds that kindness paired with self-respect, self-awareness of your boundaries and honesty about what you can and cannot do—and being assertive about it—is the magic formula. Kostelny adds: “Contrary to popular belief, a person can be both nice and ambitious. The important thing is to lift yourself up at the same time you are lifting others.”
Here’s how to make it work.
Looking back, I can now see that what I thought of as “being nice” was actually an early-ingrained trauma response that turned me into a nuclear-level people pleaser. I didn’t just want people to like me. I wanted to be so useful that nobody would ever have a reason to be mad at me. Essentially, I had confused being useful with being worthy.
At the time, it felt devastating. I had followed all the rules I thought I was supposed to follow. I worked hard. I helped. I stayed late. I said yes. I made myself indispensable. And I thought if I gave enough of myself away, eventually somebody would look at me and say, “You’ve done enough. You deserve something too.”
Instead, I got a cleaning complaint.
Being nice doesn’t mean saying yes to everything. Being kind doesn’t mean abandoning yourself. And making yourself indispensable is an awful way to find out whether someone actually values you.
These days, I’m still nice. But it’s because I want to be, not because I need to prove it to someone else.

articles.title: If You Find This Rare Pyrex Pattern, It Could Be Worth $10,000
articles.content:
Few kitchen objects are as instantly nostalgic (and, dare I say, lustworthy) as vintage Pyrex. Maybe it’s the blue mixing bowl your mother used for pancake batter, the green baking dish your great aunt brought to every holiday dinner—or, if you’re like me, the pink floral Pyrex casserole dish that caught your eye in The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel. The oval Pink Daisy dish that Midge used to transport her brisket was exactly the kind of mid-century kitchenware that made you think: I want that.
And plenty of people do. Pyrex, the Corning brand best known for its heat-resistant glass bakeware and kitchenware, became a staple in American kitchens in the 20th century. Today, vintage Pyrex has gone from kitchen cupboard staple to collector’s item, with certain patterns and pieces selling for hundreds—or, in some cases, thousands—of dollars. Suddenly, that old casserole dish isn’t just holding dinner; it might be holding a little nest egg.
The catch? That old dish isn’t valuable simply because it’s old. You need to look for the pieces collectors covet, which means you have to know which Pyrex items in your grandparents’ kitchen or in that thrift store are the ones to get excited about.
To find out how to spot a hidden gem—and estimate just how much it might sell for—I consulted three Pyrex experts: Kayleigh Davies, an antiques and collectibles specialist at Auctionet UK; Jolene Forrester, owner of vintage shop JoRetro; and Anna Pan, owner of the Etsy shop VCPvintagekitchen. Let’s dig in.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more trends, money, fun facts, humor, travel and tech all week long.
The biggest factor is simple: There aren’t many of them. According to Davies, the rarest pieces tend to be patterns that weren’t mass-produced, including prototypes and limited-production promotional pieces. Many were made for a short period or never made it into regular production.
And there’s a reason so few survived. Pyrex wasn’t sold as a collectible; it was sold to be used. Over the decades, pieces were broken, scratched, faded and separated from their lids and accessories.
But “rarity matters much less if nobody likes the pattern,” Davies adds. The most valuable pieces, she explains, are the ones that “still look great in modern homes and are worth showing off.” That combination—scarcity and desirability—creates the real collector’s market.
The appeal has broadened too. TV shows like Mad Men and The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel have helped renew enthusiasm for vintage Pyrex and the colorful mid-century aesthetic that surrounds it, perhaps contributing to more competition for pieces at thrift stores and garage sales.
If there’s one pattern that has achieved mythical status among Pyrex collectors, it’s Lucky in Love. “It’s the undisputed holy grail of Pyrex,” says Pan. The 1959 promotional casserole features green grass, four-leaf clovers and pink hearts.
In 2017, a Lucky in Love 1-quart round casserole dish donated to Goodwill of Western New York sold on the organization’s online auction site for $5,994, after 60 bidders competed for it.
According to Pan and Davies, an authenticated example can fetch from $4,000 to more than $5,000 at auction, depending on condition and the intensity of its coloration. Forrester’s estimate is considerably higher: $10,000-plus in the collector’s market. She also notes that prices for extremely rare Pyrex aren’t always publicly available.
Lucky in Love gets the headlines, but it isn’t the only Pyrex that collectors are hunting. Here are 10 other patterns and pieces worth knowing if you’re rifling through the attic, a thrift store or an estate sale—and what experts think they’re worth. Keep in mind that a pattern doesn’t have one fixed price. The exact piece, colorway, condition, completeness and place of sale can all affect the final price.
This 1960s turquoise rectangular casserole, decorated with metallic gold birds, is one of the rarest pieces on the collector’s market. Davies says it was likely made for Corning employees, with very few examples known.
How much it could be worth: $5,000 to more than $7,500, with the original decorated lid potentially adding significant value
Don’t let the delicate name fool you: Clover Berry is a serious collector’s item. Forrester specifically flags the rare 1960s pattern, distinguished by its clover-and-berry motif found only on the 2.5-quart Cinderella casserole. (By the way, the shape gets its name from the flared ends, which resemble Cinderella’s glass slipper; one serves as a handle, and the other as a pour spout.)
How much it could be worth: $6,000 for rare examples
Sometimes the biggest Pyrex find is the one that doesn’t say Pyrex. “New Mexico” is a collector name for an unusual, unmarked 1.5-quart oval casserole thought to be a test piece in the 1950s and 1960s that never went into regular production. It comes in several unusual colorways and features a geometric, starburst-like design. Because it lacks a Pyrex backstamp, it’s easy to overlook.
How much it could be worth: $6,000-plus for rare examples
Atomic Starburst has the bold, geometric look of mid-century design. But in this 1960 pattern, color is key. Davies says the turquoise version went into production, while black and peach pieces likely weren’t regularly sold to the public—making those unusual colors particularly interesting to collectors.
How much it could be worth: Up to about $1,500 for a turquoise casserole; $4,000-plus for rare black or peach designs
The Atomic Eyes chip-and-dip set is one of Pyrex’s more unusual designs, featuring an atomic-inspired eye motif. (And yes, those are apparently eyes!)
How much it could be worth: $700 to $1,000 for a complete set, which includes the metal bracket that holds the smaller bowl above the larger one
This 1968 promotional pattern features large orange-and-yellow daisy graphics—a much bolder look than many of the more familiar Pyrex patterns.
How much it could be worth: $2,000 to more than $5,000 for a pristine casserole dish with a lid
Butterprint is one of Pyrex’s most recognizable patterns, featuring Amish-inspired roosters, wheat and farm tools. The rarer Pumpkin Butterprint version, released in 1965, swaps the familiar turquoise-and-white color scheme for pumpkin orange and was offered as a Cinderella bowl set through the S&H Green Stamps program rather than sold at regular retail. Davies recently saw a four-piece set, including one chipped bowl, sell for $1,400.
How much it could be worth: $200 to $300 for an individual bowl; $1,300 to $1,750-plus for a complete set

articles.content:
If your idea of the perfect fall day involves pumpkin pancakes and a little Disney Channel nostalgia, Ashley Tisdale is right there with you. For a generation of fans, the actress and singer was everywhere—serving up laughs as Maddie Fitzpatrick on The Suite Life of Zack & Cody, stealing scenes as the fabulously over-the-top Sharpay Evans in High School Musical and giving voice to the perpetually exasperated Candace Flynn on Phineas and Ferb. These days, though, one of her favorite roles is happening off-screen: being a mom to daughters Jupiter, 5, and Emerson, 2.
In an exclusive interview with Reader’s Digest, Tisdale let us in on this very different—and decidedly cozier—chapter of her life. She shared her thoughts on motherhood, her beloved pets Sushi and Ziggy, and the fall traditions she looks forward to every year (pumpkin fans, you’re in good company). And because we couldn’t have Tisdale with us without channeling our inner Disney kid, we asked the questions longtime fans are probably wondering too: Does she ever rewatch High School Musical? And have her daughters seen their mom as Sharpay or discovered any of her other Disney alter egos?
Read on for our candid conversation with Ashley Tisdale, including details on her latest collaboration and a sneak peek at what’s next for her.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
This interview took place on Sept. 22, 2026, and has been edited for length and clarity.
Reader’s Digest: It’s cozy season! Fall has that back-to-school feel, not only for kids but also for adults. Is there anything about this time of year that makes you feel particularly nostalgic?
Ashley Tisdale: Fall is so special to me because my husband and I got engaged in August, like 14 years ago, and then we got married 12 years ago in September. Whenever this time comes around, it makes me so happy. I love a chai latte around this time. It’s so yummy. We love to make the kids pumpkin pancakes. Fall takes me back to really special moments.
Reader’s Digest: Speaking of special moments, is there something from the early 2000s that you would love to bring back—and something that you’re happy we left in the past? Personally, I’m loving the skirts-over-jeans combo.
Ashley Tisdale: It’s crazy you brought that up! [Someone I follow] was wearing a skirt over jeans in one of her social posts. I’m like, She’s bringing it back. I loved it too. Something I would not bring back is leg warmers—you know, the Abercrombie & Fitch leg warmers. That was a moment in time that should just stay there and never see the light of day again.
Reader’s Digest: What’s your ultimate fall-comfort lineup?
Ashley Tisdale: I love the movie The Holiday. Any Nancy Meyers movie is my favorite. I’ve always been a humongous fan of hers, so even my 5-year-old loves Father of the Bride.
Reader’s Digest: High School Musical is such a comfort watch too. Do you ever rewatch the films? And have your children seen them?
Ashley Tisdale: My 5-year-old has definitely watched it and loves it. I don’t watch myself very often. It’s so funny because I definitely watched Disney growing up. I like movies like Hocus Pocus. But I don’t really watch the Disney movies as much now, and we keep it to a minimum. She’s a huge fan of the movie, but there’s only so many times I can listen to the songs and watch the movies.
Reader’s Digest: How has being a mom changed the way you look back at the younger version of yourself?
Ashley Tisdale: Being a mom kind of connects me to my mom. I feel like it’s the best thing in the entire world. I love being a mom. I wasn’t someone who, when young, was like, Oh, one day I’m gonna get married and have kids. I was so focused on my work and career, and so I didn’t really think like that. I didn’t even expect it, and then obviously I got married and ended up having kids, so it’s kind of a surprise.
Mom and Dad say it all the time. They’re like, “Oh, my gosh, Jupiter is so you.” She’s definitely entertaining. It’s in her blood, and she loves musical theater and music. My husband is a composer, so she really does love music, and she’s really good at singing. I don’t want her in the business. I want her to choose it for herself if she wants to. But there is this thing in her that I see that I’m like, Wow, that’s what I probably was like.
Reader’s Digest: Fall tends to be when everyone gets back into routines after summer. What does getting your household back into a rhythm look like for you?
Ashley Tisdale: We always try to stay in a rhythm. A routine is something that I think kids thrive with, so they do have a certain bedtime. We love to vacation in the summer, but we really try to always keep them on track.
Reader’s Digest: Is there anything you always do to reset yourself at this time of year?
Ashley Tisdale: I love meditations. Sometimes in the summer, I tend to fall off. I do it every single afternoon. I try to check in and do a little five-minute meditation. It’s just so good for our nervous systems. Having kids is always crazy and chaotic. [There’s] screaming, running around and then crying. It’s a lot, so I do try to take care of myself in that way.
Reader’s Digest: During this interview, you’ve been holding one of your adorable pets, Sushi. Where did her name come from?
Ashley Tisdale: Sushi is just my love for sushi. At one point in my life, like right when I got her, I had take-out sushi. I had too many tuna rolls, so they were like, “You cannot have sushi for a minute. It was too much mercury.” So I was like, “What am I going to name her?” I’m like, “Oh, Sushi, because I can’t have it, but I love it!”
Reader’s Digest: Ziggy and Sushi are both part of the family. How would you describe their personalities, and who would you say causes the most mess at home?
Ashley Tisdale: Ziggy definitely causes the most mess. She’s a very little, anxious dog. Their personalities are really cute. Sushi is just like a stuffed animal. I swear, she just sleeps with me. She’s just cuddled up right next to me.
Ziggy sleeps with us too, but she’s at the end of the bed. She does not want to be touching you, but Sushi’s just a little lover. She’s so sweet. She’ll let the kids pick her up and everything. Ziggy’s a little bit more all over the place.
Reader’s Digest: How does enrichment fit into Ziggy and Sushi’s routine, especially when it comes to your partnership with Nylabone’s new chew toys with real meats?
Ashley Tisdale: I’m someone who cares what’s in my kids’ food and my food. So, of course, I’m going to care about what my dogs are chewing on and eating as well. Ziggy does have anxiety, and so one of the tools that trainers have told us in the past was to distract her, and that’s usually with treats and chew toys. This is just something that keeps her entertained for hours. She loves it. Chewing also helps them be calmer.
I have so much going on during the day. I have two kids. It’s crazy in the morning. It’s chaotic, and so to have just a product that you can trust to give to your dogs, keeps them happy and is also really healthy for their gums, Nylabone was a no-brainer.
Reader’s Digest: What’s next for Ashley Tisdale?
Ashley Tisdale: There are so many exciting things coming up, but I can’t share too much. My product line, Being Frenshe, just launched at Ulta, which has been such a huge goal of mine. It’s really cool to see something that I created there.
Reader’s Digest: Dogs or cats?
Ashley Tisdale: Definitely dogs.
Reader’s Digest: Mornings or nights?
Ashley Tisdale: Mornings.
Reader’s Digest: Aisle seat or window?
Ashley Tisdale: Window.
Reader’s Digest: Would you rather travel to the past or the future?
Ashley Tisdale: I was thinking about this the other day. Probably the past. I think the future would leave me with too many questions. I’ll get anxious.
Reader’s Digest: What is your favorite book?
Ashley Tisdale: The Power to Heal.
Reader’s Digest: If you weren’t an actress or singer, what would you be doing?
Ashley Tisdale: I run a company, so I definitely think I have a thing for branding. I’d probably do brand marketing.
Reader’s Digest: What advice would you give to your younger self?
Ashley Tisdale: Keep going. You’ll get there.

articles.title: Fall’s Big Debate Settled! Is It OK to Eat an Apple Right Off the Tree, or Do You Need to Wash It First?
articles.content:
When I took my kids strawberry picking over the summer, more of the juicy red fruits ended up in their mouths (and down their shirts) than in their buckets. So now, as I prepare to take them apple picking this fall, I’m fully expecting a similar experience. I mean, those apples are delicious, and even better, the kids are eating something healthy.
But should I be putting a stop to this mid-picking fruit gorging? Yes, everyone does it, but as with so many things, that doesn’t mean it’s a good idea! I don’t want to be a party pooper here, but I have to wonder if it’s actually safe or healthy to eat an apple straight off the tree. After all, I always wash my apples when I bring them home from the supermarket. Is washing equally important when you’re getting your fruit straight from the source?
To find out, I spoke with Jessica Brantley-Lopez, a registered dietitian nutritionist who also coaches organizations on food safety and sanitation. Read on to find out the answer to this fall debate—and decide if you’re willing to take the risk.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more debates, food safety, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Technically, no, it’s not ideal. “Even though [that apple] may look clean, it has been growing outdoors and can be exposed to bacteria from animals, soil, water or even people handling the fruit,” Brantley-Lopez says. “If you’re at an orchard, there may also have been agricultural sprays used on the trees.” Yep, she’s talking about pesticides. (More on that below.)
The best-case scenario? You consume something yucky. The worst case, of course, is that you get sick. “You just don’t know what that apple may have been exposed to,” she explains. “That’s why rinsing it first is such an easy step to reduce your risk.”
Since apples are growing outdoors, there are quite a few things that can make their way onto the surface of the fruit. Here are the most likely culprits.
Sure, kids may eat dirt from time to time. But do we really want them to eat it if we can prevent it? And do we want to eat it ourselves? I’d guess that the answer to both those questions is no. According to the National Library of Medicine, there’s nothing inherently poisonous or dangerous about dirt itself, but it can contain chemicals, fertilizers, parasites, fungus or toxins that could make you ill, and you might not be able to see those things on the surface of the apple.
There could be bird poop or schmutz from other animals on the apples, says Brantley-Lopez. And any contamination that comes from animals, even if it’s only a little bit, could expose you to illness-causing bacteria. When it comes to bird poop, in particular, there’s a risk of contracting psittacosis, a respiratory infection. You don’t actually need to consume the bird poop to catch this bug; it’s most commonly spread by inhaling dust that contains dried bird droppings. People who have a lot of contact with birds, like poultry workers, bird owners or pet-shop employees, are at a greater risk, but you could still get it if you pick and bite into an apple that has some of this dust on it.
Bacteria from animal contamination isn’t the only thing you need to worry about. There could be other bacteria growing on the apple, transferred from the soil or water while the apple was growing. The most harmful one is listeria, which is generally found near the stem or on the bottom of the apple, per Washington State University. Listeria can cause unpleasant gastrointestinal symptoms, according to the Mayo Clinic, but it can be much more serious for pregnant people and folks with weakened immune systems.
There was a listeria outbreak in 2014 linked to commercially produced caramel apples; the caramel coating created an ideal environment for the bacteria to grow. And while there haven’t been any outbreaks tied to fresh apples recently, it’s still something you should be aware of.
“At a busy apple orchard, you don’t know how many people may have touched that apple before you picked it,” says Brantley-Lopez. You also don’t know how recently they washed their hands. Apples are not the same as countertops or doorknobs—after all, they have a waxy surface and a certain level of moisture—but the germs that cause respiratory infections, the flu and norovirus, for instance, may survive for a few hours on the fruit’s surface if someone with one of these illnesses touched it but decided not to pick it. Then, if you ate it before washing it … well, you know how that story ends.
“Depending on the orchard, there could also be pesticide residue or other agricultural sprays on the surface of the apple,” Brantley-Lopez says. According to a 2025 report from the USDA’s National Agricultural Statistics Service, 77% of apple growers use insecticides and 75% use fungicides, so there’s a very high chance that your local orchard is using some sort of spray to protect its apples from bugs and diseases.
Eating one apple with some pesticides on it likely won’t cause any immediate harm, but long-term exposure has been associated with diseases like cancer and neurological disorders.
There could be an ant or another small bug crawling across the surface of the apple. Chances are, you’ll notice this and flick it off, but what happens if you’re distracted by your kids and you forget to look before you take a bite? Just … yuck.
Perhaps if the orchard only uses organic farming practices or doesn’t use pesticides? Unfortunately, that’s also a no. “Organic versus non-organic doesn’t really change the risk of bacterial contamination,” says Brantley-Lopez. “An organic apple can still be exposed to animals, soil, water and people handling it. And organic doesn’t always mean pesticide-free. Some approved sprays can still be used.”
Yes. “Depending on what may be on the apple, you could experience anything from mild stomach upset, nausea or diarrhea to a more serious foodborne illness,” Brantley-Lopez says. “Some bacterial infections can become severe enough to require a hospital visit.”
I mentioned some of the possible infections you could catch earlier, but what it boils down to is that you just don’t know what chemicals or contamination the apple has been exposed to when you pick it. As a result, it’s hard to say how large of a risk you’re taking by munching on it without washing it.
Yep—the old rinse ‘n’ rub is enough to reduce dirt and bacteria on the surface of the apple, says Brantley-Lopez. “Many orchards have washing stations available, sometimes right in the picking area,” she adds. “And you don’t need soap or a special produce wash. Plain running water is best.” If you’re apple picking with kids and already toting a bag with you, consider bringing a bottle of water or a small spray bottle so you can rinse off the apples before eating them.
That said, this advice applies to unbroken, unbruised apples that are still hanging from the tree. “If an apple has fallen on the ground, check it carefully for bruising, cracks or other damage,” Brantley-Lopez says. “A fallen apple isn’t automatically bad, but once the skin is damaged, there is more opportunity for contamination.” And if the apple actually looks bad, even a little, it’s best to just leave it there.
Yes, the same rules apply to apples from the grocery store. “Even if apples were rinsed during packing, they can still pick up dirt or bacteria during transportation, handling or at the grocery store,” says Brantley-Lopez.
That goes for apples you plan to peel or cook with too. “Cutting or peeling can transfer bacteria from the outside of the apple to the inside,” she explains, so it’s still important to wash it.
The bottom line: At the very least, splash some water on your apples before they make it to your mouth or your kids’ mouths.

articles.title: 6 Scientifically Backed Ways to Recover from a Bad Day When Things Just Aren’t Going Your Way
articles.content:
I recently had one of “those days.” You know the ones, where absolutely nothing goes your way and things just keep getting worse the further into it you get. After a crazy day, I forgot to pick up groceries, so I scrounged around my kitchen for something to eat, dropped an egg, and then turned around too quickly and knocked a favorite bowl to the floor, where it shattered into pieces. After quickly cleaning up, I later stepped on a rogue shard that had flown, unnoticed, out of the kitchen and onto my wood floor.
Sheesh, I thought, ready to cocoon myself in bubble wrap. Can things get worse?
I envisioned choking to death on my dinner, ingesting some other shard of ceramic or maybe slipping in the shower later that night and hitting my head. I wasn’t sure my evening could recover.
It’s a thing, this downward spiral of doom. We all do it. But do we make it worse for ourselves? And do we have the power to turn our days around, or are we cursed once the spiral begins? To find out, I spoke with experts in psychology and neurology: Patrice Le Goy, PhD, a psychologist, therapist and adjunct professor; Matthew Leahy, PhD, a licensed psychologist in private practice; and Sanam Hafeez, PsyD, a New York City–based neuropsychologist.
It turns out that the spiral is real—though also semi-self-created. “The first bad thing may happen to us,” says Leahy. “But then our brain starts helping build the case that the whole day is ruined.” It doesn’t have to be, though.
Read on to learn some surprisingly easy ways to boost your mood and make things a whole lot better—and also recognize when it’s time to call it a day.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more life hacks, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Believe it or not, yes. A day that seems to be spiraling out of control comes down to both how your brain is wired to notice threats and what’s happening chemically once it decides something qualifies as one.
Le Goy points to negativity bias. “Bad days can spiral because we often give more attention to negative things than we do to positive ones,” she says. We’ve evolved this way to protect ourselves. “Negative experiences are more likely to feel threatening, and so to stay ‘safe,’ we have to be vigilant in recognizing these threats.” Plus, we tend to focus on the facts that support our new theory that everything is a disaster, and this can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. That mindset can shift our mood and our actions, inadvertently setting us up for more negative interactions.
But there’s more to it than simply perspective. “The amygdala is heavily involved in sounding the alarm,” Hafeez says. “If your brain decides there is a threat, it signals areas such as the hypothalamus to get the body ready to respond. Your heart may beat faster, your muscles tense and your attention can narrow toward whatever seems wrong.” Once that response is underway, she explains, “it can become harder for the prefrontal cortex—the part that helps with reasoning, perspective and self-control—to have as much influence over your reaction.”
That alarm also triggers a cortisol spike, which sets off a cascade of chemicals that send inflammatory signals through the brain. At the same time, that cortisol suppresses GABA, the neurotransmitter responsible for keeping you calm. With your calming chemical suppressed and your inflammatory signals firing, your brain gets stuck in a heightened, reactive state. That feedback loop is why a single bad moment rarely stays contained to just that moment: It keeps feeding itself. It’s also why, as Hafeez puts it, “the third annoying thing that happens at 4 p.m. can feel much worse than it would have if it happened first thing in the morning,” and why something you’d normally brush off can suddenly feel like the final straw.
Sleep is certainly one of our strongest resets, but you don’t have to wait until the next morning to feel different. “A bad morning can still become a decent afternoon because the brain and body are constantly responding to what is happening in the present,” says Hafeez. “There isn’t a specific neurological point where the brain decides the entire day is ruined. Even after hours of stress, the nervous system can begin calming down when it gets signals that the immediate threat or problem has passed.”
When my own recent bad day went down, in addition to mentally listing all the other things that could go wrong, I chuckled as I envisioned myself as a slapstick comedian a la the Three Stooges or Kramer from Seinfeld, with my mishaps recast as a well-orchestrated, graceful (if goofy!) dance. Turns out, I was using a proven method for pulling myself out of the spiral. And that’s just one of the things you can do to take a beat and stop the inflammation loop when you notice your day going downhill.
“When we are able to pause and stay present, we can stop a bad moment from becoming a bad day,” says Le Goy. She calls this halt the single most important move available to you in the moment. “When we find ourselves spiraling, it is often because we are jumping ahead and making assumptions that the rest of the day will be as bad as this particular moment. When we take a beat, we can decide how we want to move forward, rather than being swept away on the negative emotion wave.”
A 2021 review in the journal Translational Psychiatry found a strong link between anxiety and depression and those who lacked the ability to notice their thoughts and feelings as passing mental events rather than absolute truths. Turning my calamity into a comedy short in my mind’s eye helped interrupt my own spiral.
Being realistic can help as well. Don’t expect you’ll do a full 180 and suddenly have a fantastic day; your mind won’t accept what it doesn’t already believe. Aim for a neutral day, one where you’re back in control of what happens. Part of that is not compounding the problem: Naming what’s actually going on (“I’m keyed up right now”) instead of escalating it into a verdict (“Everything is going wrong”) keeps one rough moment from snowballing into a ruined day.
Identifying what’s going on and calling it out can help break the spiral. Saying or writing out loud “I’m having a bad day” can be the beat you need to separate yourself from the negativity. “I feel like I’m a mess today” hits differently than “I’m a mess.”
The science backs this up. A 2022 study found that five 30-minute weekly mindfulness sessions significantly dropped serum cortisol and perceived stress levels in nursing students. Another showed that a mindfulness retreat produced bigger drops in cortisol and inflammatory markers than a comparison group who simply took a vacation with no structured practice. Rest alone didn’t move the needle; structured mindfulness did.
“If everything is irritating you, leave the room and do something random, even if it’s just walking around Target or taking a drive while blasting music,” says Hafeez. “A change of scenery can make the bad part of the day feel like it belongs to an earlier chapter rather than the rest of your day.” Even moving to a different room can be enough to interrupt the spiral.
A 2023 study put that theory to the test: 100 people took a 30-minute walk in either a natural or urban setting, and both groups showed significant, equal improvements in mood. Positive affect increased, and negative affect dropped, surprisingly with no real difference between the nature and city settings. The takeaway: Getting outside and moving your body seems to boost your mood regardless of the scenery, meaning the shift in context itself may be doing the heavy lifting.
Moving your body helps take you out of threat mode, even if it’s brief: a walk around the block, a few jumping jacks or anything else that shifts your physical state. “Get up and move, and get that stress hormone cortisol out of the body,” Leahy says. “You don’t need a workout. A brisk walk, stretching or doing something physically active can help move your attention out of your head and back into your body.”
The reason? According Hafeez, that movement gives the body “somewhere to put the energy that comes with a stress response and can help shift attention away from the stressful event.”
Experts more formally established that in a 2021 study where 83 young men did 30 minutes of treadmill exercise at varying intensities, then faced a stressful task 45 minutes later. The harder they’d worked out, the faster their bodies calmed back down afterward: Those who exercised vigorously recovered in about 81 minutes, versus 91 minutes for the light-exercise group.
